correction: Known evidence exists. Feldman et al. report statistically significant clear-sky CO 2 surface-forcing increases of 0.2 W/m² per decade at Oklahoma/Alaska sites during 2000–2010, associated with 22 ppm more CO 2. Their analysis combines measured spectra, ancillary observations and radiative-transfer calculations; fossil emissions and fires substantially contributed to the CO 2 increase. This is empirical support for the warming mechanism, not a standalone estimate of global temperature attribution.
effect: Undercuts the categorical absence-of-evidence premise supporting refusal to base policy on anthropogenic-warming concerns.
limits: The measurement is surface radiative forcing at two clear-sky sites, not direct measurement of global temperature sensitivity or the benefit of this bill. It uses model-assisted isolation of CO 2, with reported uncertainties ±0.06/±0.07 W/m² per decade; methods discuss cloud-selection effects. The author may mean no evidence he regards as convincing: later pages reject mainstream research and funding arrangements. That evaluative reading should be distinguished from the literal claim that no indications are known. No intent is inferred.
materiality_explanation: Major editorial judgment: the claimed absence of any indications is a foundational premise of the submission’s policy objection, rather than an incidental figure. The correction does not establish that any particular fuel quota is efficient or desirable.
direction_explanation: True: categorical absence makes rejection of the bill’s climate rationale appear stronger. This direction is assessed separately from materiality.

card.law_is_about: Adding wolves to federal hunting law and regulating regular hunting and targeted removals.
card.they_want: Broader regular wolf hunting, with fewer conservation-status obstacles.
card.they_claim: An absence of favourable conservation status among German wolves cannot justify opposition to regular hunting, because the whole European population is decisive.
card.the_problem: The cited judgment expressly requires local and national assessment. Cross-border exchange can support favourable status; a favourable European population does not replace the national assessment.

claim_quote.original: Ein angebliches Fehlen des GEZ der deutschen Wölfe kann also keineswegs als Begründung gegen die reguläre Bejagung des Wolfs herhalten.
claim_quote.translation_en: Translation: An alleged absence of favourable conservation status among German wolves can therefore in no way serve as a reason against regular wolf hunting.

locator.paragraph: Third body paragraph, following the reference to CJEU C-629/23 of12June2025.

request_quote.translation_en: Translation of request fragment: to call for wolf hunting

locator.paragraph: Second substantive paragraph, bold sentence identifying potential loss of open-land biodiversity as the main reason for the request.

request_quote.context: The preceding page questions why favourable conservation status plays a decisive role in the bill; the final page also seeks hunting guidelines in ordinances rather than statute.

counter_quote.original: örtlicher und nationaler Ebene bestehen und bewertet werden
counter_quote.translation_en: Translation of fragment: exist and be assessed at local and national level

correction: C-629/23 requires favourable conservation status to exist and be assessed primarily and necessarily at local and national level. Paragraph 48 expressly applies that principle to Article 14 management of AnnexV species. Paragraphs 52–64 allow relevant cross-border demographic and genetic exchange to inform that assessment, including where an isolated national population would not be viable. They do not make an unfavourable national status irrelevant merely because the wider European population is favourable.
effect: Removes the stated legal basis for dismissing the German conservation-status condition in the argument for regular hunting. It does not establish the outcome of any particular hunting application.
limits: The judgment does not require each country’s wolves to be biologically self-sufficient: paragraph 55 expressly allows continuous exchange to support favourable national status. The author’s earlier phrase about local wolves not being favourable entirely on their own is compatible with that point. The finding concerns the later categorical dismissal of German status, not the legitimacy of considering European connections. It does not determine Germany’s actual conservation status, ecological population boundaries, hunting effectiveness, the legality of every targeted removal, or the desirability of the bill. No intent is inferred.
context_and_alternatives: Read all 3 physical submission pages, including the author’s separate ecological reasons for hunting, preference for juvenile removal, and desire to place operational guidelines in ordinances.

The strongest benign reading is that the author objects to treating Germany as an isolated biological population. The cited judgment supports considering cross-border exchange, but expressly preserves the local and national legal assessment; the later categorical conclusion goes beyond that reading.

The case concerns Estonia, where wolves already fell under AnnexV. Its Article 14 reasoning is relevant to the proposed post-reclassification German framework; no claim is made that all factual circumstances are identical.
The population-size assertions and the claim that all European populations exchange genes were not independently determined here. They are not separate findings.
